A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same evolving work, retaining the adaptive-margin approach, role-playing corpus, benchmarks, and examples despite substantial reframing. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model experiments, downstream DPO results, component ablations, self-evolution experiments, and human evaluations, including general-task results in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments comparing margin variants, role-playing reward models, downstream GRPO models, and human preferences in Tables 1–3 and Figure 4.

M1.justification: v2 retains v1's loss-difference margin as AAM-LD but adds AAM-PR, which uses likelihood ratios against a reference policy. It removes the substantial self-evolution component: iterative unlabeled-data filtering, confidence-based partitioning, and targeted response rewriting. These are procedural changes beyond renaming ChARM to AAM.

E1.justification: The main coverage is retained: RewardBench and JudgeBench already appeared in v1 Appendix B, while RoleplayPref and RoleplayEval largely reappear as Charm and Charm-DialogueQuality. v2 additionally reports using 2,000 real human–AI role-playing preference pairs alongside synthetic conversations, modestly broadening the represented interaction data.

E2.justification: v2 substantially revises the general reward-model comparator set, adding GPT-4o, Claude, Prometheus2, CompassJudger, ArmoRM, OffsetBias, URM, Tulu3, and Skywork-Critic-8B. It removes Skywork-Reward-Gemma-2-27B, InternLM-20B-Reward, and Eurus-RM-7b from their corresponding comparisons. GPT-4o and Claude also become comparators for role-playing reward scoring in Table 2; the downstream dialogue baseline roster remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v1 uses 4,600/4,873 annotated seed pairs, a 20,000-sample evolution pool, and 6,864 bilingual DPO samples. v2 reports 4,000 reward-training pairs and 4,000 separate contexts for GRPO. Reward-model evaluation changes from 1,000 in-domain plus 1,000 out-of-domain samples to a 4,000-entry bilingual benchmark. Dataset preference selection also changes from reward-model scoring to human selection of the best and worst responses.

E4.justification: v2 removes v1's explicit seen-versus-unseen-character analysis and self-evolution experiments across seed sizes and iterations. It expands margin-design analysis through PR-versus-LD comparisons and SFT controls on general and role-playing benchmarks. The appendix case studies retain their scenarios but replace the proposed model's responses with GRPO outputs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The human evaluation retains five annotators and 200 test samples; relocating its description to v2 Appendix A.2 does not change uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v1's general-task AAM averages of 90.5 and 68.1 are retained as LD results, while v2 adds PR/SFT results, including 91.6 on RewardBench. The BT safety entry changes from 90.3 to 93.3. Role-playing and human-evaluation results are replaced: for example, the 32B CharacterEval average changes from 3.75 under DPO to 3.77 under GRPO. These downstream results use different training conditions and do not establish a same-setting gain.

T1.justification: v1 derives its margin from KL divergences between preferred/rejected response distributions and the model distribution. v2 replaces this reasoning with a derivation from KL-regularized RLHF to the probability-ratio margin, then develops a SimPO-inspired likelihood formulation for LD in Equations 3–10. This substantially changes the mathematical justification, although neither version supplies formal theorems.

C1.justification: v1 centers a role-playing framework combining adaptive margins and self-evolution, claiming a 13% preference-ranking improvement and the first role-playing preference dataset. v2 centers annotation-free margin calibration for subjective ambiguity, claims 2.95% general-task and 4.85% role-playing improvements, and emphasizes GRPO-based alignment. Self-evolution and the dataset's 'first' claim disappear from the stated contributions.

C2.justification: v1's discussion of alignment tradeoffs, difficulty improving character knowledge, and empathy differences is removed. v2 adds interpretations connecting poor general-purpose judging to the need for specialized subjective reward models. Its limitations replace the restriction to two reward dimensions with limited validation at larger model scales, while retaining the lack of critique modeling.

D1.justification: v2 discloses ten postgraduate-level preference annotators and non-overlap between reward-training and GRPO contexts, and changes the advertised repository from ChARM to AAM. The stated reward-training learning rate, epochs, regularization coefficient, and hardware remain unchanged. v1's downstream full-parameter/LoRA settings and learning rates disappear without comparable GRPO hyperparameter details.

R1.justification: The positioning broadens from role-playing agents to subjective reward modeling and contrasts the approach with verifiable-reward RL. Related work adds substantial discussion and citations concerning creative writing, emotional support, DeepSeek-R1, implicit rewards, SimPO, and newer evaluators. Several earlier role-playing-specific references and discussions are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around subjective ambiguity. The standalone dataset section is folded into downstream experiments, general-task experiments move from the appendix into the main narrative, human-evaluation details move into the appendix, and Further Discussion is removed. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn around the two margin formulations, and v2 adds a conceptual derivation diagram as Figure 5. v1's separate general-benchmark tables are merged and expanded into v2 Table 1; the role-reward table changes from ID/OOD columns to language columns. Self-evolution and rewriting tables disappear, while case-study displays and captions are updated.

improvement.justification: The new PR/LD and SFT comparisons better examine margin design, and broader baseline comparisons strengthen contextual evaluation. However, v2 removes explicit unseen-character evidence and provides fewer details for reproducing downstream training. It also changes the BT RewardBench safety score to 93.3 while retaining the 87.4 average, creating an unreconciled numerical inconsistency. These gains and reporting losses prevent a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
